regulatoryStandards.title: Resinous and Polymeric Coatings for Food Contact
regulatoryStandards.threshold: Total extractives < 0.5 mg/sq in of food contact surface

regulatoryStandards.title: Ceramic Ware Release of Lead and Cadmium
regulatoryStandards.threshold: Lead limit < 0.5-2.0 mg/L; Cadmium limit < 0.05-0.5 mg/L depending on vessel depth

regulatoryStandards.title: Plastic Materials Intended for Food Contact
regulatoryStandards.threshold: Overall migration limit (OML) of 10 mg/dm² of food contact area

regulatoryStandards.title: Tolerable Weekly Intake (TWI) for PFAS
regulatoryStandards.threshold: Group TWI of 4.4 ng/kg body weight per week for sum of 4 PFAS (PFOA, PFNA, PFHxS, PFOS)

regulatoryStandards.title: Safe Drinking Water and Toxic Enforcement Act
regulatoryStandards.threshold: Maximum Allowable Dose Level (MADL): Lead 0.5 µg/day; BPA 3 µg/day

materials.name: Traditional PTFE Non-Stick (Teflon / Classic)
primaryToxins: PFAS Oligomers (PFOA/PFOS legacy traces, GenX, PFHxA)
Toxic Fluoropolymer Pyrolysis Fumes (HF, TFE, PFIB at >260°C / 500°F)
materials.healthRisks: Polymer fume fever ('Teflon flu') upon overheating; chronic bioaccumulation of perfluoroalkyl substances linked to endocrine disruption, thyroid dysfunction, and elevated cholesterol; intestinal microplastic exposure.
materials.bestFor: Low-temperature egg cooking with wooden or silicone utensils only
materials.neverUseFor: High-heat searing, dry preheating empty pans, metal whisks or knives, broiling in oven
materials.saferAlternative: 3-ply 304/316 Stainless Steel or Seasoned Cast Iron
materials.scientificCitation: Cheng et al., Flinders & Newcastle Univ. (2022) 'Raman imaging for microplastics release from non-stick cookware', Sci. Total Environ.

materials.name: Sol-Gel Ceramic Non-Stick (Mineral Coating)
materials.coatings: Silicon dioxide (SiO₂) mineral network with titanium dioxide (TiO₂) nanoparticles
materials.healthRisks: Significantly safer than fluoropolymer coatings with zero PFAS risk. However, thermal shock micro-fractures accelerate sub-micron mineral particle release. Nanoparticle toxicity under prolonged ingestion remains under scientific evaluation.
materials.bestFor: Gentle medium-heat sautéing and acidic sauces under 180°C (350°F)
materials.neverUseFor: Scouring with steel wool, sudden thermal shock (running cold water onto hot pan), dishwasher cycles
materials.saferAlternative: Enameled Cast Iron or Multi-clad Stainless Steel
materials.scientificCitation: European Commission Joint Research Centre (JRC, 2021) 'Nanomaterial release from sol-gel food contact coatings'.

materials.name: Raw Uncoated Aluminum
materials.coatings: None (Bare Aluminum 1000/3000 series with natural thin oxide film)
materials.healthRisks: Soluble aluminum ions readily dissolve into food under acidic contact. Aluminum is a cumulative neurotoxic metal linked in clinical toxicology to neurological impairment, osteomalacia, and impaired renal excretion.
materials.bestFor: Dry baking with parchment paper, boiling neutral tap water (pH 7.0)
materials.neverUseFor: Cooking tomato sauce, lemon reductions, vinegar marinades, wine gravies, or sauerkraut; dishwasher cleaning
materials.saferAlternative: Anodized Hard-Coated Aluminum (sealed pore matrix) or 18/10 Stainless Steel
materials.scientificCitation: EFSA CONTAM Panel (2008) 'Safety of aluminium from dietary intake'; Al Juhaiman (2010) Food Chem. Toxicol.

materials.name: Artisan / Vintage Lead-Glazed Ceramic & Terracotta
materials.coatings: Low-fire decorative flux glaze (Lead Monoxide PbO, Cadmium Carbonate CdCO₃)
materials.healthRisks: Critical neurotoxin with no known safe blood lead level. Chronic exposure leads to permanent cognitive deficits in infants and children, maternal toxicity, renal tubular necrosis, and cardiovascular disease.
materials.bestFor: Decorative display only, or dry non-acidic grain storage (rice, dry beans)
materials.neverUseFor: Hot coffee, tea, fruit juices, tomato soups, vinaigrettes, microwave reheating, or baking
materials.saferAlternative: High-fired Vitrified Porcelain, Borosilicate Glass, or Lead-Free Certified Stoneware
materials.scientificCitation: US FDA Compliance Policy Guide Sec. 545.400 / 545.450; ISO 6486-1 Lead & Cadmium Limits.

materials.name: Food-Grade Silicone (Baking Mats & Molds)
materials.coatings: Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) elastomer with platinum or peroxide curing
materials.healthRisks: Cyclic siloxane D4 is classified under EU REACH as an endocrine-disrupting substance of very high concern (SVHC). High heat combined with lipids (butter, oils) causes measurable siloxane migration into fatty foods.
materials.bestFor: Freezer storage, ice molds, room-temperature dough kneading, spatulas for stirring
materials.neverUseFor: High-heat roasting of fatty meats above 200°C (392°F), open broiler flames, toaster ovens
materials.saferAlternative: Unbleached Parchment Paper, Glass Baking Dishes, or Stainless Steel Baking Sheets
materials.scientificCitation: German Federal Institute for Risk Assessment (BfR, 2020) 'Silicone in food contact'; Danish EPA Study No. 177.

materials.name: Unlined Bare Copper & Brass
primaryToxins: Toxic Verdigris (Basic Copper Carbonate & Copper Acetate)
materials.healthRisks: Acute copper intoxication causing severe gastroenteritis, nausea, projectile vomiting, hepatic toxicity, and hemolysis. FDA Food Code strictly prohibits unlined copper contacting foods with pH below 6.0.
materials.bestFor: High-sugar non-acidic jam candy making (sugar binds water), whipping egg whites (stabilizes foam)
materials.neverUseFor: Cooking sauces with tomatoes, wine, vinegar, lemon, beer, or sour cream
materials.saferAlternative: Tin-Lined Copper or Stainless-Clad Copper Cookware (Mauviel / Falk)
materials.scientificCitation: FDA Food Code § 4-101.14 'Copper, Use Limitation'; Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR).

materials.name: Food-Grade Stainless Steel (18/8 & 18/10, AISI 304/316)
materials.coatings: Self-healing Chromium Oxide (Cr₂O₃) passive boundary layer
materials.healthRisks: Extremely safe for 98% of the population. Trace nickel migration can trigger flare-ups in individuals with severe diagnosed Systemic Nickel Allergy Syndrome (SNAS). Cr(III) is an essential trace nutrient.
materials.bestFor: Everyday cooking, boiling, high-acid tomato sauces, searing, deglazing with wine
materials.neverUseFor: Long-term soaking in concentrated salt brine or bleach (causes localized chloride pitting)
materials.saferAlternative: Nickel-Free 430 Ferritic Stainless Steel (for diagnosed nickel-allergic individuals)
materials.scientificCitation: Kamerud et al. (2013) J. Agric. Food Chem. 'Stainless steel cookware and toxic metal release'.

materials.name: Seasoned Cast Iron & Carbon Steel
materials.coatings: Polymerized unsaturated vegetable oil patina (carbonized lipid matrix)
materials.healthRisks: Non-toxic and beneficial for preventing dietary iron deficiency. However, contraindicated for people with genetic Hemochromatosis (iron overload disorder). Extended acid simmering strips seasoning and creates strong metallic taste.
materials.bestFor: High-heat searing, steaks, smash burgers, cornbread, stir-frying, deep frying
materials.neverUseFor: Simmering tomato marinara or wine reductions for over 30 minutes; dishwashers; wet storage
materials.saferAlternative: Enameled Cast Iron (Le Creuset / Staub) for acidic stews
materials.scientificCitation: Brittin & Nossaman (1986) J. Am. Diet. Assoc.; Sharma et al. (2021) Eur. J. Clin. Nutr.

materials.name: Melamine Tableware & Resin Dinnerware
materials.healthRisks: Melamine crystal precipitation causes renal tubular injury, nephrolithiasis (kidney stones), and chronic kidney failure. Formaldehyde vapor is a respiratory toxin and designated human carcinogen.
materials.bestFor: Cold snacks, outdoor picnics, dry ambient-temperature finger foods
materials.neverUseFor: Microwaving under any circumstances, boiling soups, hot coffee, serrated knife steak cutting
materials.saferAlternative: Tempered Glass (Duralex, Corelle) or Vitrified Ceramic
materials.scientificCitation: US FDA Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition (CFSAN) 'Melamine in Tableware Questions and Answers'; Lund & Petersen (2006).

materials.name: Plastic Food Storage & Microwave Containers (PP #5, PC #7)
materials.coatings: Polypropylene (PP) or Polycarbonate (PC) with UV stabilizers and plasticizers
primaryToxins: Microplastics and Nanoplastics (billions per cm² in microwave)
materials.healthRisks: Disrupts endocrine hormone receptors (estrogen/androgen signaling), alters metabolic adipogenesis (weight gain/insulin resistance), and introduces sub-micron plastic debris capable of crossing cell membranes.
materials.bestFor: Cold refrigerated meal prep, dry pantry storage, salad transport
materials.neverUseFor: Microwave heating (especially with butter, oils, or tomato sauces), boiling water immersion
materials.saferAlternative: Borosilicate Glass Food Storage with silicone/bamboo lids (Pyrex, Glasslock)
materials.scientificCitation: Hussain et al., Univ. of Nebraska-Lincoln (2023) Environ. Sci. Technol. 'Assessing Nanoplastics Released from Microwave Heating'.

conditions.label: Brand New / Pristine (No Visible Wear)
conditions.description: Factory barrier intact with smooth uncompromised surface.

conditions.label: Light Wear / Hairline Scratches
conditions.description: Surface scratches visible under reflection; coating or glaze still continuous.

conditions.label: Moderate Scoring / Dull Loss of Gloss
conditions.description: Noticeable utensil drag marks, loss of non-stick release, micro-pitting in glaze.

conditions.label: Severe Flaking / Deep Gouges / Chipped Glaze
conditions.description: Exposed substrate metal, peeling black flakes, cracks exposing porous ceramic bisque.

temperatures.label: Cold / Ambient (<25°C / <77°F)
temperatures.description: Refrigeration, room temperature salad storage, cold drinkware.

temperatures.label: Gentle Warm / Low Simmer (60-100°C / 140-212°F)
temperatures.description: Slow cooker, warming trays, gentle water poaching, tea/coffee.

temperatures.label: Medium Sauté / Boiling (150-180°C / 300-350°F)
temperatures.description: Everyday skillet frying with cooking oil, boiling pasta sauces.

temperatures.label: High Sear / Baking (200-240°C / 400-464°F)
temperatures.description: Oven roasting, stir-frying, deep frying, searing poultry.

temperatures.label: Extreme Heat / Dry Preheating (>260°C / >500°F)
temperatures.description: Empty pan preheat on high flame, broiling, flash searing steaks.

acidities.label: Neutral / Oily (pH 6.5 - 7.5)
acidities.description: Water, milk, cooking oils, plain meats, rice, pasta, eggs.

acidities.label: Mildly Acidic (pH 4.5 - 6.0)
acidities.description: Coffee, onions, chicken broth, beer, lightly fermented dressings.

acidities.label: Strongly Acidic (pH < 4.0)
acidities.description: Tomato sauce, vinegar marinades, lemon/lime juice, wine reductions, sauerkraut.

durations.label: Quick Exposure (<10 Minutes)
durations.description: Quick fry, boiling water, flash sauté.

durations.label: Standard Cooking (15 - 45 Minutes)
durations.description: Normal meal preparation, skillet dinner, standard baking.

durations.label: Extended Simmer / Braise (>2 Hours)
durations.description: Slow-simmering ragù, bone broths, chili, braised roasts.

durations.label: Overnight Contact / Storage (>12 Hours)
durations.description: Storing leftovers in the pan, overnight marinating in container.
